threads: Thread tags: SMSC S/So (M/C: none); British Values IL/MR (D/RL/T: none).
thread_rationale: S: reflect on the range of work without requiring personal disclosure. So: compare role information and listen when task talk is chosen. IL: choose an accessible response mode and request help or a pause. MR: value different roles and support needs without ranking workers or narrowing choices through stereotypes.
prepare: Provide the four sector source cards, twenty occupation cards, five role-type labels, an administration job-family strip and a blank four-sector map for each learner. Use the cards as the preselected information source; no online research or current labour-market data is required. Prepare a separate demonstration map and the complete adult key. Offer a chunked card set and a four-sector Floor scaffold with two occupation options per row. Keep eight preselected support cards ready: HC1, HC3, CO1, CO3, ED2, ED5, RE1 and RE4; this set spans all five role types. Have a previous profile or shortlist available only if it exists and the learner chooses to use it privately. Otherwise use the supplied fictional retrieval prompt. Books are the default; reader, scribe, usual aid and typing are normal ways of working. Arrange quiet adult check-ins, extra processing time and a regulation break with a supported return.
activity: Retrieve from the previous profile/shortlist/enquiry task without assuming completion or asking for public personal answers. Model the distinction between a sector, an occupation and a job family using the source cards. During guided analysis, compare work tasks, map examples across four sectors, notice five overlapping role types and test the cross-sector administrator example. For independent application, create a four-sector map with accurate occupation placements in each sector, a task-based reason for one placement in each sector, one occupation that can occur across sectors and an administration job-family explanation. Include frontline, technical, professional, support and management examples across the map using the supplied bank; these are overlapping work descriptions, not fixed ranks. Keep first placements, actual prompts and any revised thinking. Reflect individually and update the Careers Portfolio or action plan only with actual work.

task_choices.title: Build a sector and occupation map
task_choices.reading: Use the supplied sector and occupation source cards to compare where work happens and what people do. The same occupation can occur in more than one sector. Keep your own first choices, reasons and changes.
instructions: Use all four sector rows and map occupations within each. Add further roles to show the range of work.
Use a work task from a source card to explain one placement in each sector.
Across your map show frontline, technical, professional, support and management work.
Add an occupation in more than one sector and explain why it fits both.
Explain one job family and complete the sector/occupation exit check.
task_choices.answer: Use the complete map key. Each sector’s five supplied role examples are valid in their stated contexts. Administrator can cross all four; other roles can cross sectors with a plausible stated workplace context and reason. Accept an evidence-based alternative rather than treating cards as exclusive. The exact core outcome requires the sector/occupation distinction and mapping within at least four sectors. Record the other map features separately, and retain partial core evidence if the four-sector demand or distinction is not yet shown.

cases.text: A care service employs an administrator to organise appointment records and pass messages. Is health and care the sector or the occupation?
cases.judgement: Health and care is the broad sector; administrator is the occupation. The task evidence is organising records and messages.
cases.next_step: Ask privately for the sector and occupation separately.

cases.text: A construction organisation employs an administrator to organise project records. Must an administrator work only in health and care?
cases.judgement: No. The same occupation can work in construction too; administration is a job family crossing sectors.
cases.next_step: Ask which task stays similar and which workplace sector changes.

hinge: Private individual check during guided analysis: a retail organisation has an administrator who keeps staff records. Which is the sector: retail or administrator? Expected: retail is the sector, administrator the occupation. Ask for the task clue. If unsure, use the prompt ladder and model only the first distinction. Parallel check: an education setting has a technician who prepares equipment. Expected: education is the sector, technician is the occupation; preparing equipment is the task. If still unsure, use the four-sector Floor scaffold and record actual help and incomplete demand. No cold calling or inference from a group answer.
prompt_ladder: Point to the place or instruction.
Model the first step only, then return the task.

adaptations.Cognition and Learning: Use explicit instruction and a separate worked sector–occupation–task example, then fade the model. Chunk the cards and map one row at a time. Use the source vocabulary bank, a clear four-row scaffold and a private check after modelling.
adaptations.Communication and Interaction: Reader, scribe, typing, pointing and the usual aid are normal ways of working. Allow extra processing and a private response. Rehearse a purposeful task question if useful; no cold calling or compulsory pair talk. Normal access stays available when answer scaffolds fade; record access separately from answer prompts.
adaptations.SEMH: Predictable five-phase lesson, calm retrieval and regulation break with a supported return. Personal profile retrieval is voluntary; use the fictional prompt if preferred. Value different occupations without ranking learners or demanding a final career choice.
adaptations.Sensory and Physical: Use large clear print, reading strip or usual overlay, uncluttered cards and a single-row view. Staff may position cards or scribe. Typing and access aids are normal; no physical job performance or colour-only distinction.
adaptations.EAL: Preteach sector, occupation, task and job family with the model cards. Plan in any language. Offer a private read-aloud, familiar-language explanation, pointing and sentence stems, with actual help recorded.

misconceptions.wrong: Sector and occupation mean the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: A sector is a broad area of work; an occupation is a particular kind of job. Retail is a sector; checkout assistant is an occupation.

misconceptions.wrong: Each sector has one kind of worker, and an occupation can belong to only one sector.
misconceptions.correction: One sector contains many occupations and overlapping role types. An administrator can work in several sectors; administration is a related job family, not a sector.

ta_focus.I do: Check sector/occupation/task language and model source use on a separate example. Prompt a card clue rather than supplying an answer. Reader/scribe/typing as agreed; fade the model when secure.
ta_focus.We do: Chunk comparison across the four sectors, take individual private hinge responses and use the parallel check after reteaching. Clarify role-type overlap and the cross-sector administrator.
ta_focus.Independent: Log participation and individual evidence. Support source selection and one row at a time; prompt reasons instead of supplying placements. Offer a regulation break and return-to-learn. Fade prompts where secure and record any unmet four-sector demand.

Sector and occupation mean the same thing. A sector is a broad area of work; an occupation is a particular kind of job. Retail is a sector; checkout assistant is an occupation.

Each sector has one kind of worker, and an occupation can belong to only one sector. One sector contains many occupations and overlapping role types. An administrator can work in several sectors; administration is a related job family, not a sector.
